newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian unveils plan to stem losses.
newsitem.headline: Canadian unveils plan to stem losses.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp, struggling to survive amid heavy losses, said on Friday it would add capacity on foreign flights, seek wage cuts from employees and ask for concessions from its U.S. shareholder, AMR Corp.

Canadian, which said its year-to-date financial results were much worse than expected, said it could face a serious cash crunch in the first quarter of 1997 and that a string of losses threatened its survival.

"Our continuing operating losses are threatening the company's viability," Canadian Chief Executive Kevin Benson said in a statement. "Our 1996 business plan assumed modest revenue growth, which the entry of new carriers has now made unachievable."
Canadian, which has not posted an annual profit this decade, said it lost C$49 million ($36.7 million) in the first nine months of 1996 versus a year-ago loss of C$65.4 million ($49.1 million).

Calgary-based Canadian -- Canada's second-biggest airline -- said it had C$110.8 million ($92.1 million) in cash on hand at the end of the third quarter. But continued operating losses and high debt repayments in the next six months could wipe out reserves by the first quarter of 1997.
Canadian said its proposed restructing would involve doubling service to the United States and boosting Asian service by 20 percent, in moves that would take advantage of its expanded Vancouver hub.
Canadian's money-losing Paris and Frankfurt routes would be scrapped.
In Canada, where the carrier faces brutal price competition from no-frills upstarts Greyhound Air and WestJet Airlines, Canadian will cut capacity by 11 percent.
Canadian said it also planned to make better use of its smaller Canadian Regional jets to service domestic destinations in order to wring more much-needed cost savings from its fleet.
Up to 250 jobs will be eliminated under the plan, which would also ask employees to take a 10 percent wage cut.
The carrier last year struck deals with unions representing many of its 16,400 employees aimed at saving C$125 million ($94 million) a year in labour costs.

Canadian's survival plan also envisages saving C$70 million ($53 million) by asking AMR Corp., which holds 33 percent of the airline, to reduce fees for overhead, reservation services and other payments. Fort Worth-based AMR, the parent of American Airlines, receives about $100 million each year from Canadian.
AMR said it remained committed to its stake in Canadian and would consider "all reasonable Canadian requests for assistance."
Canadian said it would ask employees and unions for their cooperation in the strategy and to indicate their support by the end of this month.
